title: Regression: Predicting Numbers
subtitle: What is a house worth? Linear regression read in dollars, why a model with too many knobs memorizes, the complexity tax of ridge and lasso, the log trick, and the residual plot that shows where the model is wrong

objectives.title: Fit and Read a Linear Regression
objectives.description: Coefficients are slopes in business units: $107 per square foot on Ames, and only $55 once quality is in the model. You'll learn to read them holding everything else fixed, and to stop reading them as causes.

objectives.title: Pick the Right Error Metric
objectives.description: MAE is the typical miss in dollars, RMSE makes big misses count extra, R² is the share explained compared with guessing the average, and MAPE breaks near zero. Which one you report depends on who is asking.

objectives.title: Regularize With Ridge, Lasso & Elastic Net
objectives.description: Give linear regression 100 houses and 154 columns and it memorizes them, then misses new houses by $300K. Ridge and lasso add a complexity tax; lasso switches useless features off entirely, which is feature selection for free.

objectives.title: Diagnose With Residuals
objectives.description: Residuals vs. predicted: a fan says take the log of the target, a curve says a missing pattern, a far dot says look at that house. The plot that separates a model that works from one that merely runs.

agenda.title: From Yes/No to How Much
agenda.description: Five sessions of yes/no; tonight a number. Zillow's 2021 exit from home buying (more than $540 million in write-downs) frames the stakes. How to grade a number: the residual, MAE and RMSE on three houses, and the guess-the-average baseline.
bulletPoints: Misses of $10K, $10K and $100K: MAE $40K, RMSE $58K. RMSE makes the big miss count extra
Baseline: guess $181K for every house, typical miss (MAE) $55K, RMSE $74K, R² 0. Every model must beat that

agenda.title: One Feature, Then Two
agenda.description: Price against living area: the least-squares line, its slope in dollars, and the residuals drawn as red lines. Then add quality and watch the price of a square foot fall by half: what 'holding everything else fixed' means.
bulletPoints: price ≈ $19K + $107 × sq ft; R² 0.54; typical miss $36K
With quality in the model a square foot is worth $55: big houses also tend to be better built. Describe, don't claim causes
Play first: Station 1 of the House Price Explorer. Can you beat least squares by hand?

agenda.title: All 79 Features, and the Memorizer
agenda.description: The Session 3 pipeline turns 79 features into 255 columns; linear regression cuts the typical miss to $18K. Then the overfitting demo: on only 100 houses the model has more knobs than houses, fits them perfectly, and fails on new ones.
bulletPoints: 100 houses, 154 columns: training R² 1.00, test RMSE about $300K, four times worse than guessing the average
Ridge on the same 100 houses: about $30K

agenda.title: Break
agenda.description: Stretch, coffee, argue about what a garage is worth.

agenda.title: Ridge, Lasso & the Log Trick
agenda.description: Regularization as a complexity tax, alpha as the tax rate, cross-validation to choose it. Ridge shrinks, lasso selects. Train on log(price) so misses become percentages. Then turn lasso's dial until the model fits on one page.
bulletPoints: Typical miss: ridge $16K, ridge on log price $15K, lasso on log price $14K (LassoCV keeps 116 of 255 columns)
A strict lasso keeps 21 features for about $4K more RMSE: quality, size, age, garage, condition. A realtor's checklist

agenda.title: Residuals & the Metric Menu
agenda.description: Residuals vs. predicted for linear regression and lasso: one house priced at $569K that sold for $275K, and the biggest lasso misses, mostly new homes sold before they were finished. Then the metric menu: which number for which audience.
bulletPoints: When one house fools every model, look at the house. Unfinished new homes are a segment the model doesn't know
MAE to operations and sellers, RMSE when big misses hurt, MAPE with care and never near zero, R² to compare models

agenda.title: Your Turn & HW3, Part 2
agenda.description: Four questions in the notebook: drop Neighborhood and price the location, turn the lasso dial, write a three-sentence metric memo, and (optional) try gradient boosting on the same pipeline. Then HW3 Part 2.
bulletPoints: HW3 Part 2: a leak-proof Ames pipeline with ridge or lasso, due Mon Nov 16 together with the threshold part from Session 5
Next: decision trees and random forests, the first model that needs no scaling at all

activities.title: What Is a House Worth? Regularized Regression on Ames
activities.description: 1,460 house sales in Ames, Iowa, with 79 features. Build a leak-proof pipeline that predicts log(price), let LassoCV choose the penalty, and report the error in dollars a buyer would understand.

steps.title: Frame it
steps.description: Unit: one house. Target: sale price (modeled as log). Horizon: at listing. Decision: our offer price. Baseline: the average price, typical miss $55K.

steps.title: Reuse the pipeline
steps.description: Session 3's ColumnTransformer, wrapped in a prep() function so each model gets a fresh copy. Train on np.log(price).

steps.title: Let CV pick alpha
steps.description: LassoCV(cv=5) at the end of the pipeline. Count how many columns survived, then try a stricter Lasso(alpha=0.01) and read its survivors.

steps.title: Report in dollars
steps.description: Predict on the test set, np.exp the predictions back to dollars, then MAE and RMSE in dollars. Plot residuals vs. predicted and look at the five biggest misses.

codeBlock.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, make_column_selector
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, root_mean_squared_error

houses = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harslan/isom-835/master/public/data/ames_housing.csv')
y, X = houses['SalePrice'], houses.drop(columns=['Id', 'SalePrice'])
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=835)

def prep():   # the Session 3 recipe
    numbers = Pipeline([('fill', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')), ('scale', StandardScaler())])
    text = Pipeline([('fill', SimpleImputer(strategy='constant', fill_value='missing')),
                     ('onehot', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore', min_frequency=10))])
    return ColumnTransformer([('num', numbers, make_column_selector(dtype_include='number')),
                              ('text', text, make_column_selector(dtype_exclude='number'))])

model = Pipeline([('prep', prep()), ('model', LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=835, max_iter=20_000))])
model.fit(X_tr, np.log(y_tr))                 # train on log(price)
pred = np.exp(model.predict(X_te))            # back to dollars before grading

print(f'Baseline MAE (guess the average): ${mean_absolute_error(y_te, np.full(len(y_te), y_tr.mean())):,.0f}')
print(f'Lasso MAE: ${mean_absolute_error(y_te, pred):,.0f}   RMSE: ${root_mean_squared_error(y_te, pred):,.0f}')
coef = model.named_steps['model'].coef_
print(f'{(coef != 0).sum()} of {len(coef)} columns survive')

activities.discussionNote: LassoCV keeps about half the columns and cuts the typical miss from $55K to about $14K. Turn the tax up to alpha = 0.01 and 21 features survive: quality, living area, year built, garage, condition, fireplaces. The list reads like a realtor's checklist, which is the point: a regularized linear model is the most explainable strong model you will ever ship. Then look at the biggest misses: an unusual sale that fools every model, and new homes sold before they were finished. The model knows least about the houses where a mistake costs the most.

takeaways.text: A linear coefficient is a slope in business units, holding other features fixed — not a cause, and not comparable across features until you standardize.
Ridge shrinks, lasso selects. A complexity tax stops a model from memorizing; cross-validation picks the tax rate. A strict lasso with 21 surviving features is a model a client can read.

Metrics are for audiences: MAE for the typical miss, RMSE when big misses hurt, R² to compare models, MAPE never near zero. And always look at the residual plot: it shows where the model is wrong, and where that will cost you.
